1:
Keil frames the verse as the opening of the last stage: in the first month of the fortieth year the whole congregation assembled again at Kadesh, in the desert of Zin, to begin the march to Canaan. Wesley proves the date from what follows — the next station was Mount Hor, where Aaron died in the fifth month of that year — and adds that Moses gives no exact journal of all that happened in the wilderness, but only of what was most remarkable, and especially of the first, second and fortieth years. Ellicott is less certain. He would render the opening words Now the children of Israel came, since the interval between the preceding chapters and this one is unknown; and though it has commonly been supposed that the fortieth year is meant, some hold the journey to be the same as one mentioned earlier in this book and in Deuteronomy, so that the arrival at Kadesh fell in the first month of the third year, after the departure from Sinai. He warns besides that no conclusion about the length of the stay can be drawn from the word rendered abode, which elsewhere covers a short sojourn as easily as a long one.

Gill measures the silence the verse passes. What is related here followed the sending of the spies and the business of Korah not immediately but thirty-eight years after, and this was not the congregation that came out of Egypt, whose carcasses had by then fallen in the wilderness as had been threatened, but a new generation; of the interval we have very little account excepting their journeyings, by which it appears there were eighteen stations between the camp from which the spies were sent and the place they now came to. Calvin explains the omission differently: many intermediate stations are named elsewhere and not here, perhaps because from the time God compelled them to draw back they had made no advance for thirty whole years but wandered by circuitous paths, whereas at this point they began to direct their journey straight towards Canaan. Clarke notes a smaller question of names: Calmet contends this desert of Zin is not the wilderness of Sin where Israel had its eighth encampment, the two being spelt differently in the original — though Clarke replies that this is no positive proof, since letters of the same organ are frequently interchanged in all languages, and particularly in Hebrew.

On Miriam the commentators reckon up a long life and a mixed record. Calvin infers that she must have been a girl of ten or twelve when Moses was born, since she was able to provide so adroitly for his safety, and so reached about a hundred and thirty — an unusual length of life, and especially for a woman. Clarke agrees on the age and adds what later writers made of her: they represent her as a type of the Virgin Mary, as having preserved a perpetual virginity, as legislatrix over the Israelitish women as Moses was over the men, and as having a large portion of the spirit of prophecy; Eusebius reports that her tomb was still to be seen at Kadesh, near the city of Petra, in his own time. She died about four months before Aaron and eleven before Moses, so that these three, the most eminent of human beings, died within the space of a single year. Henry sets her service beside her fault. After thirty-eight years of tedious marches, or rather tedious rests, the armies of Israel had at last set their faces towards Canaan again; and Miriam, a prophetess and an instrument of much good, who when Moses and Aaron went before the people with their rod went before them with her timbrel in praising God for his wondrous works, and therein did them real service, had once been a murmurer, and so must not enter Canaan.
2:
Gill reads the want of water as deliberate: it was so ordered for the trial of this new generation, to see whether they would behave better than their fathers had in a like circumstance the first year they came out of Egypt. Clarke states the outcome in a sentence: the same occurrence befell them at Kadesh as had formerly befallen their fathers at Rephidim, and as the fathers murmured, so also did the children. Ellicott offers three ways the shortage may have arisen: Kadesh may have comprised a considerable portion of the wilderness of Zin, with water in some parts of the district and scarcity in others; or the supply may have proved insufficient for so great a multitude; or the miraculous supply given at Rephidim may have continued, with intermissions, up to this time and been suddenly withdrawn to try the faith of the Israelites. Wesley prefers a reason of another kind: the water that had followed them through all their former journeys began to fail here because they were now near countries where water might be had by ordinary means, and God would not use extraordinary means lest he should seem to prostitute the honour of miracles.

Gill notices what the timing of the quarrel says about the people. They contended with Moses in a wrangling and litigious manner, showing no reverence to his person on account of the dignity of his office and the many favours they had received; and they did it at a moment when, instead of quarrelling, they should have condoled with him on the loss of his sister, and bewailed their own loss of a prophetess and a leader. Calvin judges the second rebellion far worse than the first. When they had already experienced that it was in God's power to extract plenty of water from the barren rock, why do they not implore His aid, and why does that marvellous interference not recur to their minds? They rebel in words against Moses and Aaron but direct their complaints like darts against God Himself, deeming it a very great injustice that they had been brought into the desert — as if they had not in their own impious obstinacy preferred the desert to Canaan, and so deserved to pine there in want of everything. Wesley puts the aggravation shortly: their sin was much greater than their parents', because they should have taken warning by their miscarriages and by the terrible effects of them, which their own eyes had seen.

Whom the murmurers mean by the brethren who died before the Lord bears on the chapter's date. Keil denies that Korah's company can be meant, since the verb used for dying would be wholly inapplicable to their destruction, and refers the words to those who had died one by one during the thirty-seven years. Ellicott argues the other way. The reference seems to be to the plague that broke out after the insurrection of Korah, the language being very similar to what is recorded there, and the verb twice used in this verse occurring in that history and in only one other place in the last four books of the Pentateuch. He reports the inference some draw from it — that the plague must have been recent rather than forty years past, since the word fathers would otherwise have been more applicable than brethren, and the question why have ye made us come up out of Egypt is more natural from men who left Egypt as adults than from a generation largely born in the wilderness. But these considerations, he judges, are not entitled to much weight: the older portion of the congregation, who would naturally be the spokesmen, would call those who perished under Korah their brethren whether the event was recent or not, and the words rendered why have ye brought up may as properly be rendered why did ye bring up.
4:
Gill hears in the complaint a forgetting of what Egypt had been. They represent the matter as if they had been forced out of Egypt against their wills, or at least overpersuaded to do what they had no inclination to — though they had been in the utmost bondage, their lives made bitter by it, so that they cried by reason of their oppression; and all this was forgot. He adds Aben Ezra's remark that the word used here is a strange one, showing the confusion they were in. Calvin explains the withdrawal as flight: probably Moses and Aaron fled in fear, the tabernacle being a kind of refuge from the violence of the people. Still, when they throw themselves upon their faces, he understands them to have prayed not only for protection from the wrath of their enemies but that God would calm these madmen by some appropriate remedy. Their agitation appears to have deprived them of their ordinary self-restraint; and God does not try their faith and patience here as He often did elsewhere, perhaps seeing them too much overwhelmed to persevere inflexibly in pious zeal and care for the public good, so that the appearance of His glory was a support for their weakness in extremity.

From that support Calvin draws the chapter's lesson in advance. The example shows how earnestly God should be entreated constantly to support us with new supplies of His grace, since otherwise the boldest would fail at every moment: the invincible resolution of Moses had so often overcome every obstacle that there seemed no fear of his falling, yet the conqueror in so many struggles at length stumbles in a single act — whence we should the more carefully bear in mind the apostle's exhortation, that because it is God which worketh in us both to will and to do of his good pleasure, we should work out our own salvation with fear and trembling. On the command itself he hears a rebuke. By the sight of the rod God would recall so many miracles, well fitted to awaken confidence for the future, as if He were uplifting the standard of His power; and the order to speak to the rock is not unattended with a severe reproach, as if He had said that in the lifeless elements there was more reason and intelligence than in men themselves. It was much to be ashamed of that the rock, as if it could hear, should obey God's voice while the people to whom the Law had been given remained in deafness and stupidity.

Which rod was taken from before the Lord is an old question. Keil states flatly that it was the rod with which Moses performed the miracles in Egypt, laid up in the sanctuary, not Aaron's which blossomed. Ellicott lays out both sides: some suppose from the rod's being taken from before the Lord that Aaron's is meant, since that was the one kept before the testimony; but the natural presumption that it was the rod with which the miracles in Egypt, at the Red Sea and at Rephidim were wrought is confirmed by two things — Aaron's name is not mentioned in the command until after the rod, and Moses is afterwards said to have smitten the rock with his own rod. Wesley leaves the question open, allowing it may have been either Aaron's rod or that of Moses, since it is likely the wonder-working rod was laid up in some part of the tabernacle, though not in or near the ark where Aaron's blossoming rod was put. Gill decides with the Targum of Jonathan for the rod of miracles — not Aaron's rod, miraculous for its blossom and fruit, as some Jewish writers think, but the rod of Moses, with which he had smitten the rock at Horeb when the Israelites wanted water as they did now.
10:
What exactly Moses did wrong is the chapter's hardest question. Clarke answers by enumeration. God had commanded him to take the rod and speak to the rock, but Moses did not think speaking sufficient and smote it without any command to do so; he smote it twice, which indicated a great perturbation of spirit and want of attention to the presence of God; he let his spirit be carried away by the people's disobedience and spoke unadvisedly with his lips, calling them rebels; and he did not acknowledge God in the miracle about to be wrought, but took the honour to himself and Aaron in asking whether they should fetch the people water out of the rock. So they did not properly believe in God nor honour him before the people, since in their presence they seem to doubt whether the thing could possibly be done; and as Aaron was consenting, he is excluded with him. Wesley finds the infidelity in the same two places — the smiting, and that twice, when he was not commanded to smite once, and the doubtfulness of the question — but qualifies it: they did not doubt the power of God, only his will, whether he would gratify these rebels with a further miracle.

Calvin approaches the question from the other end, by first defending Moses. He was perplexed between hope and doubt, yet would never have obeyed so promptly in a matter so arduous if he had been without faith; he and Aaron had recently hidden themselves in alarm, so that it was no slight task to call back the people from whom they had fled and voluntarily encounter their madness. We scarcely perceive anything reprehensible in the matter, Calvin admits, yet since God declares that the fall of Moses displeased Him we must abide by His decision rather than our own — whence we learn that our works, on whose surface nothing but virtue appears, often abound in secret defects that escape the eyes of men but are manifest to God alone. The fault he traces to unbelief, that species of sin being expressly named in God's answer, and finds it chiefly in the question about fetching water, by which Moses seems to reject as impossible what God had promised: he weighed what the people had deserved rather than estimating God's power by His word. The psalm's verdict he takes the same way: the prophet does not excuse Moses but shows that through the people's wickedness he was carried away by inconsiderate fervour — whence we should learn that when angered by the sins of others we must beware lest a temptation of the opposite kind take possession of our own minds. Keil guards the sentence: the want of firm confidence through which both sinned was not actual distrust in the omnipotence and grace of God.

Gill records what tradition made of the double blow. At the first stroke the rock brought out only some drops, as Jarchi conjectures, which is why Moses smote again; and the Targum of Jonathan says that the first time it dropped blood and the second came much water — which, could it be credited, would make the agreement between this rock and Christ manifest, since from his pierced side came blood and water. Ellicott notes a difference of vocabulary between the two miracles: at Rephidim the rock is spoken of under one Hebrew word only, in the present narrative invariably under another, and in the psalm which refers to both, both are used. Keil reads the closing formula strictly — it does not imply that the place received the name of strife-water, but that the water God brought out of the rock received it — and finds God sanctifying Himself in two ways at once, shaming their unbelief by the miraculous gift and punishing Moses and Aaron for the weakness of their faith.
14:
Keil explains why the embassy was needed: Israel wished to enter Canaan from the east across the Jordan, not from the south, where the steep mountain ranges presented obstacles difficult if not insuperable, so Moses sent from Kadesh to ask of the kindred nation a friendly and unimpeded passage — reminding the king of the relationship, the descent into Egypt, the oppression endured there and the deliverance out of it, and promising to keep to the king's way, without turning to the right hand or the left. Gill notices that the title has changed since Israel last dealt with that country: Edom was sometimes governed by kings and sometimes by dukes, and at the Red Sea we read of the dukes of Edom, whereas here, thirty-nine years later, of a king — though who he was is not certain, Bishop Usher taking him for Hadar, the last of the race of kings named in Genesis, as Clarke also does.

Henry sets out the embassy in four parts. They claim kindred, since both nations descended from Abraham and Isaac and their fathers were twin brothers, so that for relation's sake they might reasonably expect this kindness. They give the history: Israel had been abused by the Egyptians and so ought to be pitied by their relations, and wonderfully saved by the Lord, so it was the Edomites' interest to ingratiate themselves with a people so much heaven's favourites. They beg a passport — and here Henry pauses, for though God himself in the pillar of cloud was Israel's guide, and they might on that ground have justified passing through any man's land, God would have this respect paid to the Edomites, to show that no man's property ought to be invaded under colour of religion: dominion is founded in providence, not in grace. So when Christ was to pass through a Samaritan village, to whom his coming was likely to be offensive, he sent messengers before his face to ask leave; those who would receive kindness must not disdain to request it. Lastly they give security for good behaviour, undertaking to keep the high road and not so much as use a well without paying — which Wesley glosses as the pits digged for private use, not common rivers, free to all passengers.

Calvin explains why God restrained a people who could easily have taken what lay nearest. It would seem hard to leave a country close at hand untouched and seek a more distant abode, but there were two reasons: it was unjust and by no means humane to assail their kindred, both nations descending from Isaac, circumcision being common to them as a mark of the same origin; and, weightier still, it was unlawful to cast the children of Esau out of a possession obtained by the same right by which Canaan was promised to Jacob's posterity, so that it would have been sacrilegious audacity to overthrow the prophecy of Isaac by which Esau was declared possessor of a rich and fertile soil. Wesley identifies the angel of the message as the Angel of the Covenant, who appeared to Moses in the bush and afterward in the cloudy pillar, and not Moses himself — partly because Moses was sending the message, and partly because another angel above Moses conducted them, whose mention was likely to give the embassy more authority. Clarke notes that the king's high way occurs here for the first time and appears to have been a public road made by the king's authority at the expense of the state; Ellicott supposes it led through the broad Wady el Ghuweir, celebrated for its pasture and springs. Henry lays the refusal to two causes: the Edomites' jealousy of so numerous an army, and the old enmity of Esau, who hated Jacob because of the blessing — a hatred revived now that the blessing was ready to be inherited.
19:
Calvin is uncertain whether a second embassy was sent, or whether we have here the relation of one and the same expedition; the sum either way is that the Israelites tried every means to obtain a free passage, so that their repulse might appear the harsher — and that God by this test would prove the obedience of His people. As for the Edomites, though by rashly taking up arms they drew on themselves a just destruction, God spared them for a time, not freely pardoning but deferring their punishment, as He is wont, until its due season. Keil observes that the narrative runs ahead of itself: the statement that Edom came out with much people and a strong hand anticipates the historical order, since the Edomites cannot have come at once with an army on the track of the messengers to block the road along their border. Clarke measures the refusal against custom. Every king has a right to refuse passage through his territories to strangers, but at a time when emigrations were frequent and universally allowed, it was both cruelty and oppression to refuse a comparatively unarmed and inoffensive multitude who were their own near kinsmen — though it appears only the Edomites of Kadesh were unfriendly, since Deuteronomy shows that those who dwelt in Mount Seir treated Israel hospitably, and this cruelty is strongly reprehended by Obadiah.

Gill counts the departure a mercy. They journeyed from Kadesh not directly but after some time there, buying provisions of the Edomites; and the whole congregation is said to have journeyed thence, not one lost by the king of Edom's coming out against them — they went out complete and perfect, safe and sound. Ellicott would reorder the clauses — they journeyed from Kadesh, and the children of Israel, even the whole congregation, came unto Mount Hor — and takes the insertion of the whole congregation, as in the chapter's first verse, to denote that the people were dispersed through much of their wilderness life and gathered only on particular occasions. Keil locates the mountain: it stood on the border of Edom, is placed by Josephus near Petra and by Eusebius and Jerome likewise, and is identified by modern travellers with Mount Harun on the north-western side of Wady Musa — a cone irregularly truncated, with three ragged peaks, of which the north-eastern is the highest and carries the Muhammedan tomb of Aaron, from which the mountain takes its name.

Henry hears the chapter close as it opened. It began with the funeral of Miriam and ends with that of her brother Aaron, for when death comes into a family it often strikes double: Israel had not improved the former affliction, and therefore soon after God took away their priest, to try whether they would lay that to heart. Wherever we go, death attends us. In the summons itself he finds displeasure and mercy together. Aaron must not enter Canaan, having failed at the waters of strife, and the mention of it must have gone to the heart of Moses, who knew himself perhaps the guiltier of the two; yet Aaron, though he dies for his transgression, is not put to death as a malefactor by a plague or by fire from heaven, but dies with ease and in honour — not cut off from his people, as the expression usually runs of those who die by the hand of divine justice, but gathered to his people, as one who died in the arms of divine grace. Henry finds a type in it: Aaron must not enter Canaan, to show that the Levitical priesthood could make nothing perfect, that being reserved for a better hope, since those priests could not continue by reason of sin and death, whereas the priesthood of Christ, being undefiled, is unchangeable — and to it, which abides for ever, Aaron must resign all his honour.
23:
Calvin reads Aaron's death as the execution of a sentence. God wished to show that He had not threatened him and Moses in vain, as children are threatened; for had Aaron died without such a prediction, since from his extreme age he might have seemed merely to discharge the debt of nature, the people would have taken it as nothing. But when in the death of one man the condemnation of their common guilt is manifested, such severity against the high priest — who had before propitiated God towards them all by his intercession — must have been a sharp spur, since it must needs have suggested that God was no longer to be trifled with, before whom not even this sacred dignity could escape punishment. Wesley hears the human note: so these two dear brothers must part, and Aaron must die first, though Moses is not likely to be long after him — only for a while, a little while, are they separated. On the phrase used for the death Gill notes that being gathered to one's people is a periphrasis of death, used in common of good men and bad, without regard to the persons or the places men go to; Ellicott adds that it does not refer to the place of sepulture.

Why the successor was named while Aaron still lived Calvin explains by two dangers. First, the perpetuity of the priesthood was secured; second, the people were kept from taking upon themselves, with their usual temerity, an election depending on the will of God alone — for unless Eleazar had been appointed while his father lived, the office might have fallen into disesteem, since the high dignity of any individual is often odious, and we know this people's audacity in innovation. Lest they should take a priest from another tribe at their own caprice, it was well that the man of whom God approved should be firmly established, and received without controversy as the true and lawful one. Calvin then turns to what the scene cost Aaron, and finds his faith there. He cedes not only his office but his life; had he not been persuaded that an inheritance was laid up for him in heaven he would not have migrated so calmly from the world, and since he composes himself to die as if lying down on his bed, his mind was beyond doubt lifted to the hope of a blessed resurrection. His faith was probably elevated further when he saw the testimony of God's grace, on which the safety of the people depended, made to rest on the person of his son — for it was exactly as if the image of the Mediator were set visibly before his eyes.

The transfer Clarke explains as a form of law. Stripping Aaron was in effect depriving him of his office, and putting the clothes on his son implied a transfer of it; such a transfer was called investing, or clothing, as removing a person from office was termed divesting — and among the Catholics, and in the Church of England, the same method is used in degrading ecclesiastics, whence such a degradation is called by the common people stripping a man of his gown. Ellicott marks the symmetry: the same hands that had invested Aaron with the sacred garments were employed in divesting him of them, in both cases by the express command of God. He takes the removal of the robes as typical of the future disannulling of that priesthood when a priest after the order of Melchizedek should arise, and quotes Dean Stanley that the succession was made through that singular usage, preserved to the latest days of the Jewish hierarchy, by the transference of the vestments of the dead high priest to the living successor. Keil records simply that Moses executed the command, and Aaron died upon the top of the mountain.
28:
Wesley turns the stripping into a memento mori. Death will strip us: naked we came into the world and naked we must go out, and we shall see little reason to be proud of our clothes or marks of honour if we consider how soon death will strip us of all our glory and take the crown off from our head. He notes how immediately it followed — presently after Aaron was stripped of his priestly garments he laid him down and died — and draws a wish from it: a good man would desire, if it were God's will, not to outlive his usefulness; why should we covet to continue longer in this world than while we may do God and our generation some service? Keil records the bare facts: Aaron died at a hundred and twenty-three, mourned by all Israel thirty days. Ellicott sets the scene beside the other death that closes the Pentateuch: both brothers were excluded from the land of promise by transgression and both died upon a mountain top, but whereas Moses died in solitary grandeur and the place of his burial was unknown, Aaron ascended in the sight of all the people and died in the presence of Moses and Eleazar.

Clarke draws two conclusions from Lightfoot. The first is an indisputable proof that the earthly Canaan was not the utmost felicity at which God's promises aimed, since the best men among them were excluded from it — to which he adds the fathers' remark that neither Moses the representative of the law, nor Miriam the representative of the prophets, nor Aaron the representative of the priesthood could bring Israel into the promised land, that being reserved for Joshua, who was in name and in conduct the lively type of our Lord and Saviour. The second is a piece of arithmetic. They wandered by many stations from Kadesh-Barnea until they came to Kadesh-Barnea again, seven or eight and thirty years after they had first left it; and though it was only eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir, they made it above thrice eleven years' journey. Gill explains how the people learned of the death, since they did not see the body: by the relation of Moses, and by such circumstances as not seeing Aaron come down whom they had seen go up, and seeing Eleazar wearing his garments. The mourning lasted the month out, the length of public mourning among the Jews, as Josephus relates.

Calvin finds in that mourning a fault the nation shared with almost all others. It has been an error common to nearly every people and age, but reigning peculiarly among the Israelites, to pay honour to God's holy servants rather after their deaths than in their lives: they had frequently wished to stone Aaron and raised great tumults to cast him down from the dignity in which God had placed him, and now, forgetting their malignity, they lament for him dead. Whether a month's mourning was praiseworthy he doubts, since it could not but aggravate grief, men being naturally too much inclined to excessive sorrow, and the hope of a better life availing to mitigate it — whence he infers that those who give way to immoderate grief have scarcely any taste of eternal salvation. Yet believers have another cause for mourning, to exercise themselves both in the fear of God and in the hope of the future resurrection, and on that ground the custom has not unreasonably been received. Since death is a mirror of God's curse upon the whole human race, it is profitable, whenever any of our own dies, to mourn our common lot and humble ourselves beneath God's hand; and mourning directed to its proper end in a manner unites the living with the dead, so that in death itself the communion of the new and immortal life shines forth.
